plainLanguage: In one study, people who trained with compound lifts gained more bench press strength than people who trained with isolation lifts, but their body composition changed the same amount.
qualifiers: The outcome is the exercise the multi-joint group trained and the single-joint group did not, so the difference confounds adaptation with practice of the test.
No pectoralis-specific size or strength measure was taken, so this says nothing about chest muscle growth.
The contrast is whole programmes differing in every exercise, not two chest exercises.
Both groups performed an identical concurrent soccer routine.
Strength adaptation transfers only partly beyond the trained task, which is why the task-specificity qualifier is mandatory here.

conditions: 8 weeks, three sessions weekly, work volume equated individually; multi-joint chest work was the bench press, single-joint chest work was the pec deck machine and incline dumbbell fly
scope.population: 36 young male amateur soccer players with no previous resistance-training experience, in pre-season

sourceLinks.locator: Results and Table 2 (1RM bench press 8.1 versus 10.9 per cent, ANCOVA p < 0.05); Table 1 (exercise lists per group)
Title and Abstract (generality of strength adaptation)

statement: In one eight-week volume-equated trial, a programme built entirely from multi-joint exercises produced a larger increase in one-repetition-maximum bench press than a programme built entirely from single-joint exercises (10.9 versus 8.1 per cent, p < 0.05), with no difference in body composition.
